focus: A pre-norm sublayer reads a normalized copy of the stream but writes into the unnormalized stream. The stream is the embedding plus every earlier branch output, so its scale can grow with depth. A post-norm model renormalizes after every addition. Xiong Lemma 2 states exactly this for their setting: the expected squared norm is flat in depth for Post-LN and grows linearly for Pre-LN.

Theorem 1 bounds one thing: the gradient of the last FFN layer. It is independent of \(L\) for Post-LN and shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{L}\) for Pre-LN. Lemma 3 gives the mechanism: the Jacobian of a normalization scales like \(1/\|x\|\), and \(\|x\|\) is what differs. Read the assumptions before you trust the picture: initialization only, uniform attention (query and key weights zero), one head, square weight matrices and Gaussian inputs.

Two ways to hold the stream scale: scale each residual output projection by \(1/\sqrt{2L}\) (two branches per block), or keep a fixed small standard deviation and rely on normalization. OLMo 2 dropped a depth-dependent scheme for a flat standard deviation of 0.02 and reports growth exponents closer to 0 for activations and gradients. That is one report on its own models with its own measurement, and it compares against OLMo-0424's layer-index scheme, not against uniform \(1/\sqrt{2L}\).

OLMo 2 changed several things as a package (reordered norm, QK-norm, z-loss, initialization). Section 3.3.2 says reordered norm and QK-norm 'in isolation' do not give good results, so the report cannot attribute the gain to any one of them.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the mean square of the stream after \(N\) residual branches whose outputs are independent, zero-mean and each of variance \(v\), on an input of variance \(\sigma_0^2\): \(\sigma_0^2 + Nv\). Scaling each branch by \(1/\sqrt{N}\) gives \(\sigma_0^2 + v\) for every \(N\). Then, on your own pre-norm decoder with random token IDs and no training, record the stream mean square after every block for \(L = 4, 16, 64\), with and without scaling the attention output projection and FFN down projection by \(1/\sqrt{2L}\). Labeled example, not a target: with a toy decoder (width 128, 4 heads, FFN width 344, RMSNorm, normal initialization with variance \(2/(\text{fan-in} + \text{fan-out})\), 4 sequences of 64 random tokens, mean of 3 seeds, PyTorch 2.14.1 on CPU) the final mean square was 2.38, 10.6 and 56.7 for \(L = 4, 16, 64\) unscaled, and 1.14, 1.15 and 1.15 scaled. Growth in the unscaled runs was faster than linear in \(L\) (the increment per sublayer rose from 0.17 to 0.30 to 0.43), so the independence assumption does not hold exactly. Expect the scaled values to stay flat and the unscaled ones to grow.
traps: Reading Theorem 1 as a layer profile. It bounds the last layer only. In the same toy at \(L = 64\) with post-norm, the FFN down-projection gradient norm was 0.160 at the last block and 7.4 at the first, the opposite order to 'gradients are large near the output', while the last-layer value stayed near 0.15 to 0.16 for \(L = 4, 16, 64\) as the theorem says. Pre-norm gave 0.108, 0.049 and 0.022 at the last block. Measure the whole profile in your own model.

Treating the OLMo 2 stability result as evidence for one component. Its Table 1 and Section 3.3.2 describe a package, and Equation 2 in Section 2.1 writes \(\operatorname{MLP}(x)\) where Table 1 and the Section 3.3.2 table use the intermediate state \(h\). Follow the table.

Calling a flat curve of stream norm 'stable'. The stream scale at initialization says nothing about training, and the final norm hides a growing stream from the output head. Compare the stream scale at several points in training before you claim a depth effect.

selfTest.q: Why does a pre-norm model need a final norm before the output head?
selfTest.a: The stream is unnormalized and its scale depends on depth and position in training. Without a final norm the logits would carry that scale. The final norm restores a fixed scale before the head.

selfTest.q: \(N\) branch outputs are independent, zero-mean, each of variance \(v\), and are added to a stream of variance 1. What is the variance after the additions, and after scaling each branch by \(1/\sqrt{N}\)? What changes if the outputs are perfectly correlated?
selfTest.a: \(1 + Nv\), and \(1 + v\) after scaling. If the \(N\) outputs are perfectly correlated, the sum has variance \(N^2 v\), so growth is quadratic in \(N\) and \(1/\sqrt{N}\) scaling no longer holds the scale.

selfTest.q: Why does Theorem 1 give a last-layer gradient that falls like one over the square root of depth for Pre-LN but is flat for Post-LN?
selfTest.a: The Jacobian of the final normalization scales like \(1/\|x\|\). In Pre-LN the squared norm of the stream grows linearly with \(L\), so the gradient shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{L}\). In Post-LN the input to the normalization has a depth-independent norm.

selfTest.q: A colleague says the OLMo 2 report shows depth-scaled initialization is worse than a flat standard deviation. What does the report actually compare?
selfTest.a: A flat standard deviation of 0.02 against OLMo-0424's scheme, which scaled output projections by a factor that depends on the layer index. It measured growth exponents and spike scores in its own setup, alongside other changes. It does not test uniform scaling by one over the square root of twice the layer count.

study.title: Small-Scale Proxies for Large-Scale Transformer Training Instabilities (arXiv:2309.14322v2)
study.locator: Section 3.1 (3.1.1 attention logit growth and 3.1.2 output logit divergence), Figures 1 to 4
study.depth: Stop before Section 3.2. The muParam, warmup and depth experiments belong to later units.

focus: LayerNorm is RMSNorm applied to the mean-centred input. The two agree exactly when the feature mean is zero (same \(\epsilon\) and gain, no bias). Add a constant to every feature and LayerNorm does not change, while RMSNorm rescales and keeps the offset. Dropping the mean removes one reduction and the bias parameter, and the claim that this makes the model faster is about memory traffic, not FLOPs.

The Jacobian of a normalization is \(1/r\) times a projection, so gradients through a norm scale like one over the input scale. That is the mechanism behind Xiong's Lemma 3 and behind the learning-rate sensitivity in Wortsman et al.

Softmax is invariant to adding a constant to all logits, so cross-entropy is flat along that direction and nothing stops the offset from drifting. z-loss, \(c(\log Z)^2\) with \(Z = \sum_i e^{z_i}\), adds a gradient \(2c \log Z\) times the softmax along it. QK-norm bounds the attention logits directly: after per-head RMSNorm with unit gains each query and key has norm \(\sqrt{d_h}\), so \(|z| \le \sqrt{d_h}\) before the gains.

Name each hotspot with its failure. Squares in float16 overflow when \(|x| \ge 256\), because \(256^2 = 65536\) exceeds the float16 maximum 65504. bfloat16 keeps the float32 range but has 8 bits of precision, so logits in \([64, 128)\) are rounded to multiples of 0.5. Naive sequential accumulation stalls once the running sum reaches 256 in bfloat16. Library reductions and fused norm kernels accumulate in a wider type, so you must check your own code, not the library's.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the RMSNorm Jacobian at \(\epsilon = 0\) and show that its largest singular value is \(1/r\) with \(r = \sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_i x_i^2}\) and that \(x\) itself is mapped to zero. Show \(\operatorname{LayerNorm}(x) = \operatorname{RMSNorm}(x - \bar{x})\). Then derive the z-loss gradient with respect to the logits, \(\operatorname{softmax}(z) - \text{onehot}(y) + 2c \log Z \cdot \operatorname{softmax}(z)\), and check it against autograd in float64 for \(z = [2, 0, -1]\), \(y = 0\), \(c = 10^{-4}\): the gradient is \([-0.15584, 0.11424, 0.04203]\) with \(\log Z = 2.16985\). Finally, in PyTorch 2.14.1 on CPU, take a float16 vector of 4095 ones and one entry 300. A hand-written `x.pow(2).mean()` gives `inf` and the normalized row is all zeros. After `x.float()` the entries are 0.2086 and 62.59. `torch.nn.functional.rms_norm` on the same float16 input returns finite values because the library upcasts.
traps: Testing a hotspot through the library function instead of your own code. In the check above `torch.nn.functional.rms_norm` is safe in float16, and `torch.ones(10000, dtype=torch.bfloat16).sum()` gives 9984 (a rounded result of a wider accumulation), but a Python loop adding ones in bfloat16 stops at 256. The hand-written norm and reduction in your block are what can fail.

Claiming QK-norm 'fixes' attention logit growth without a baseline run at the same learning rate. Wortsman et al. show growth at high learning rates in small models and relate it to the quadratic dependence of logits on parameter norms; they call that a hypothesis. Run both variants at several learning rates.

Trusting a fused z-loss kernel. OLMo 2 Figure 8 shows a fused implementation and a plain PyTorch one that agree in the forward pass and diverge in the backward pass, and the report suspects precision. Compare gradients, not only the loss value.

selfTest.q: When do LayerNorm (no bias) and RMSNorm give the same output, and what happens to each when you add a constant to every feature?
selfTest.a: They agree when the input already has zero mean over the feature axis, with the same \(\epsilon\) and gain. Adding a constant leaves LayerNorm unchanged, because it subtracts the mean. RMSNorm still divides by the new root mean square, so the constant remains in the output at a different scale.

selfTest.q: Why can't cross-entropy alone stop all the logits from drifting upward together, and what does z-loss add?
selfTest.a: Cross-entropy depends only on logit differences, so adding \(\delta\) to every logit leaves the loss and its gradient unchanged while \(\log Z\) rises by \(\delta\). The term \(c(\log Z)^2\) is not shift-invariant and adds the gradient \(2c \log Z \cdot \operatorname{softmax}(z)\), which pulls \(\log Z\) toward 0.

selfTest.q: After per-head RMSNorm with unit gains, what is the largest possible attention logit \(q \cdot k / \sqrt{d_h}\)?
selfTest.a: \(\sqrt{d_h}\). Each normalized vector has root mean square 1, so norm \(\sqrt{d_h}\), and Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the dot product by \(d_h\). Learned gains multiply the bound, so the observed maximum can exceed \(\sqrt{d_h}\).

selfTest.q: An activation vector in float16 has largest entry 200. Is a hand-written RMS computation safe? What if the entry is 260?
selfTest.a: At 200 the square is 40000, below the float16 maximum 65504, so the square is finite. At 260 the square is 67600, which overflows to `inf`, and every output of that row becomes 0. The threshold is 256 because \(256^2 = 65536 > 65504\).

selfTest.q: Two runs differ only in whether QK-norm is on, and the QK-norm run reaches a lower loss at one learning rate. What else must hold before you credit QK-norm?
selfTest.a: Several seeds at that learning rate, a learning-rate sweep for both variants (the best learning rates may differ), and the same data order and token budget. A single run at one learning rate cannot separate the mechanism from learning-rate sensitivity.

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook, Appendix B: From Parameters to Memory
study.locator: Section 1 (Parameters) and Section 2 (Activation Memory)
study.depth: Section 2 lists the tensors a forward pass produces, not the tensors autograd saves, and omits two that a SwiGLU feed-forward network saves. Use it for the layout and recount with hooks. Stop before Section 3.

focus: A gated feed-forward network has three \(d \times h\) matrices and an ungated one has two \(d \times 4d\) matrices, so equal parameters means \(3dh = 8d^2\) and \(h = \tfrac{8}{3}d\). Shazeer's Section 3.1 states the same match as 3072 to 2048 at \(d = 768\): \(2 \cdot 768 \cdot 3072 = 3 \cdot 768 \cdot 2048\).

Real configurations round the width. For \(d = 4096\) the exact width is 10922.67 and OLMo 2 uses 11,008, so the gated block has 0.78% more parameters than a 4x ungated block. State the counted parameters of both variants in any comparison.

Parameters and matmul FLOPs match; saved activations do not. For one token, an ungated GELU feed-forward network at width \(4d\) saves \(2h + d = 9d\) elements for backward (input, pre-activation, activation), while the gated one at width \(\tfrac{8}{3}d\) saves \(4h + d \approx 11.67d\) (input, two projections, the activated gate and the product).

Shazeer's Table 1 reports means with standard deviations of 0.004 to 0.010 for four 65,536-step runs and single values at 524,288 steps. The 0.003 gap between GEGLU (1.633) and SwiGLU (1.636) at the longest run is smaller than that run-to-run spread. The setting is T5 span-filling with Adafactor and no dropout.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, for width \(d = 4096\): derive \(h = 8d/3\), then count a 4x GELU feed-forward network (\(2 \cdot 4096 \cdot 16384 = 134{,}217{,}728\) parameters) against the gated one at width 11,008 (\(3 \cdot 4096 \cdot 11008 = 135{,}266{,}304\)), a difference of 1,048,576 or 0.78%. Then for a block with 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head size 128 and \(d = 4096\), derive 41,943,040 attention parameters (67,108,864 for multi-head) and 4096 bytes of bfloat16 KV cache per token per layer. Finally, wrap each feed-forward module in `torch.autograd.graph.saved_tensors_hooks`, count unique saved non-weight tensors for \(d = 96\) at widths 384 (GELU) and 256 (SwiGLU), and match \(9d\) and \(11.67d\) elements per token (864 and 1120). The two modules both hold 73,728 parameters. Measured in PyTorch 2.14.1 eager mode, float32.
traps: Calling a width match a cost match. Equal parameters and equal matmul FLOPs leave saved activations and elementwise work different (about 1.3 times the saved elements here), and a recompute or fused-kernel policy changes the saved set again. Report which cost you matched.

Recounting with the notebook's Section 2 recipe. It lists produced tensors, counts a feed-forward block as \(2BSD + 2BSF\) and rounds the gated block's \(6.33BSD\) up to \(8BSD\). Autograd also saves the activated gate and the gated product, and a count from hooks is the check.

Reading the 8/3 rule as exact. Rounding the width to a multiple of 64, 128 or 256 changes the parameter count, and the 4x baseline in the A1 SiLU ablation matches the gated width only 'approximately'.

selfTest.q: Why is the matched gated width \(\tfrac{8}{3}d\) and not \(\tfrac{2}{3} \cdot 4d\) of something else?
selfTest.a: It is the same number: three matrices of \(d \times h\) must equal two matrices of \(d \times 4d\), so \(3h = 8d\). Equivalently the ungated width \(4d\) is reduced by a factor of 2/3.

selfTest.q: A model with width 4096 uses a gated feed-forward width of 11,008. By how many parameters per layer does it differ from a 4x ungated network?
A SwiGLU and a GELU feed-forward network have identical parameter counts. Which one saves more activations for backward, by how much, and why?
selfTest.a: SwiGLU, about 11.67d against 9d elements per token (1.3 times). It saves the shared input, both projections, the activated gate and their product, while GELU saves the input, the pre-activation and the activation.

selfTest.q: Shazeer's Table 1 has GEGLU at 1.633 and SwiGLU at 1.636 after 524,288 steps. What can you conclude about their ranking?
selfTest.a: Nothing firm. The gap is 0.003, the 65,536-step runs have standard deviations of 0.004 and 0.010, and the longest runs are single values. The paper recommends SwiGLU on the whole table, not on that gap.

selfTest.q: Per token and per layer, how many KV-cache bytes does a bfloat16 model with 8 KV heads of size 128 need, and what is the cache for one 8192-token sequence in a 32-layer model?
selfTest.a: \(2 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 4096\) bytes per token per layer. Over 32 layers and 8192 tokens that is \(4096 \cdot 32 \cdot 8192 = 1{,}073{,}741{,}824\) bytes, exactly 1 GiB (1.07 GB).

focus: KV elements per token per layer: MHA \(2 n_h d_h\), GQA with \(n_g\) groups \(2 n_g d_h\), MQA \(2 d_h\), MLA \(d_c + d_h^R\). For DeepSeek-V2 (128 heads, \(d_h = 128\), \(d_c = 512\), \(d_h^R = 64\), 60 layers) that is 1,966,080 against 34,560 elements per token, a ratio of 56.9, equal to GQA with 2.25 groups (Table 1).

MQA and GQA reduce the bytes loaded per decoded token. The attention multiply-adds are unchanged, because every query head still attends over every cached position. Shazeer's ratio of memory access to arithmetic drops from \(\Theta(n/d + 1/b)\) to \(\Theta(1/d + n/(dh) + 1/b)\), and only the \(n/d\) term shrinks, by a factor \(h\).

RoPE sits between the query projection and the key up-projection, so \(W^{UK}\) cannot be absorbed into the query projection. DeepSeek-V2 carries position in extra query heads and one shared rotated key of size \(d_h^R\) that is also cached. That shared key is why the cache is \(d_c + d_h^R\), not \(d_c\).

Conversion direction matters. Replicating each GQA key and value head into a full MHA gives an identical model. Mean pooling the heads of an MHA checkpoint into groups does not, which is why the GQA paper uptrains (5% of the original compute for T5 XXL) and finds mean pooling beats taking the first head or random initialization (Figure 4).
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the four cache formulas and the DeepSeek-V2 numbers above. Then implement MLA with decoupled RoPE in float64 for \(B = 2\), \(T = 9\), width 48, 4 heads, \(d_h = 12\), \(d_c = 16\), \(d_h^R = 8\). Path 1 materializes the keys and values from the latent. Path 2 absorbs \(W^{UK}\) into the query and \(W^{UV}\) into the output projection, so attention touches only the latent and the shared rotated key. Both paths apply a causal mask and must agree: the maximum absolute difference was 1.3e-15 in my run (PyTorch 2.14.1, CPU), and anything under 1e-10 passes. Cache elements per token per layer for these shapes: 24 for MLA, 96 for MHA. Also check that expanding GQA key and value weights into an MHA gives a difference of exactly 0.0, and that mean pooling a random MHA does not.
traps: The Modern LLM Notebook (Section 6, commit 979eecf) counts the decoupled RoPE key as \(\text{num\_heads} \times d_r = 8192\) elements per token per layer and prints MLA as 8704 elements (3.8 times smaller than MHA), while saying the RoPE side path is 'only a small portion'. DeepSeek-V2 Equation 15 defines one key shared by all heads, so the cache is \(512 + 64 = 576\) elements.

Trusting a shape-only exercise. Notebook Exercise 3 passes if the output has the right shape and is finite, and its `SimpleMLA` has no causal mask. Add the absorbed-path equality test and a future-token test before you call the layer correct.

Reading the quality results as portable. MQA reports a small loss in 2019 translation and language modelling. GQA reports T5 encoder-decoder summarization, translation and question answering. DeepSeek-V2's Appendix D.1 matches parameters by changing depth, and its claim that MLA beats MHA comes from the authors' own models. None is a decoder ablation at your scale.

selfTest.q: A decoder has 32 layers, 8 KV heads of size 128 and bfloat16 caches. How many bytes does each token add, and what would 32 KV heads cost? What is the cache of one 4096-token sequence in each case?
selfTest.a: \(2 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 \cdot 32 = 131{,}072\) bytes per token with 8 KV heads and 524,288 with 32. For 4096 tokens that is 512 MiB and 2 GiB.

selfTest.q: Does GQA reduce attention FLOPs during decoding? What does it reduce?
selfTest.a: No. Each query head still computes scores against every cached position, so the multiply-adds are unchanged. It reduces the keys and values stored and loaded per step, which shrinks the \(n/d\) memory-to-compute term in decoding.

selfTest.q: Which conversion is exact: GQA to MHA by copying each group's key and value weights to all its query heads, or MHA to GQA by averaging the heads in a group? Why does the other one need training?
selfTest.a: Copying is exact, because attention with replicated keys and values is what GQA computes. Averaging keys and values changes every head's attention scores and values, so the converted model computes a different function. Uptraining lets the model adapt.

selfTest.q: Why does MLA cache \(d_c + d_h^R\) rather than \(d_c\)?
selfTest.a: Applying RoPE to the up-projected keys would put a position-dependent rotation between the query projection and \(W^{UK}\), blocking the absorption and forcing recomputation of all prefix keys. DeepSeek-V2 therefore uses extra query heads and one shared rotated key of size \(d_h^R\) for position, and that key must be cached as well.

selfTest.q: In absorbed MLA decoding with \(d_c = 4 d_h\), roughly how does the number of multiply-adds per head per cached position compare with materialized keys and values, ignoring the RoPE part?
selfTest.a: About four times larger: scores and the weighted sum run in the latent dimension \(d_c = 4 d_h\) instead of \(d_h\). MLA trades extra arithmetic for a much smaller cache, so it moves decoding toward compute-bound.

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook: Long Context Extrapolation
study.locator: Sections 4 to 9 (RoPE, why extrapolation fails, position interpolation, NTK-aware) and Section 12 (how to validate long context)
study.depth: Do not use Section 10 or the `yarn` branch of `ExtrapolatableRoPE` as a description of YaRN (see the traps).

focus: RoPE rotates each pair \(2i, 2i+1\) of a query or key by the angle \(p\,\theta_i\) with \(\theta_i = b^{-2i/d}\), so \(\langle R_m q, R_n k\rangle\) depends on \(m - n\) only. With explicit position IDs this also holds for any common offset, which is what a KV cache and a packed batch rely on.

Relative encoding does not make extrapolation safe. The PI paper shows a fitted attention-score function that stays within \([-1, 1]\) on the trained range and reaches values above 8000 outside it (Figure 2), and calls the RoFormer decay bound too loose to rule that out. YaRN's account: pairs whose wavelength \(\lambda_i = 2\pi b^{2i/d}\) exceeds the trained length \(L\) never complete a rotation in training, so long-range angles are new to the model.

The four maps, with \(s = L'/L\). PI divides positions by \(s\). NTK-aware sets the base to \(b' = b\, s^{d/(d-2)}\), which leaves the first pair unchanged and divides the last pair's frequency by exactly \(s\). NTK-by-parts leaves pairs with \(L/\lambda_i > \beta\) alone, divides pairs with \(L/\lambda_i < \alpha\) by \(s\) and ramps between (\(\alpha = 1\), \(\beta = 32\) for Llama). YaRN adds one scalar on the attention logits, \(1/t = (0.1 \ln s + 1)^2\), applied by scaling both queries and keys by \(\sqrt{1/t}\).

Fine-tuning needs differ. PI needs a short fine-tune and is worse than the other maps without one in the small run of the reproduce step. NTK-aware works better than PI without fine-tuning, but the YaRN paper reports that fine-tuning with it gives inferior results to PI. With dynamic scaling the scale follows the current length, so cache keys before applying RoPE.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive \(\langle R_m q, R_n k\rangle = \langle R_{m-n}\, q, k\rangle\) pair by pair, then compute for head size 128, \(b = 10000\), \(L = 4096\), \(\alpha = 1\), \(\beta = 32\) the number of pairs with \(L/\lambda_i < 1\), with \(L/\lambda_i > 32\) and in the ramp (18, 21 and 25 of the 64 pairs). Compute the NTK-aware base for \(s = 8\) (82,684.6) and check that the last pair's frequency ratio is 0.125 exactly. Implement RoPE with explicit position IDs and check in float64 that for random \(q, k\) the score at positions (2, 5) equals the score at (12, 15), and that with PI at \(s = 4\) the score at (40, 100) equals the unscaled score at (10, 25), so distance 60 looks like distance 15. Then measure: labeled example, not a target, from a 4-layer pre-norm decoder (width 128, 4 heads, head size 32, base 10000, byte-level text, 2500 steps at length 128, cosine schedule, one seed, PyTorch 2.14.1 on CPU, no fine-tuning at the longer lengths). Mean held-out next-byte loss in nats at length 128 was 1.119. At lengths 256, 512, 1024 and 2048 (\(s = 2, 4, 8, 16\)) direct extrapolation gave 2.008, 2.979, 3.657 and 4.241, PI 2.985, 3.802, 4.152 and 4.619, NTK-aware 1.437, 2.058, 2.789 and 3.580, NTK-by-parts 1.807, 2.568, 3.041 and 3.606, and YaRN 1.825, 2.613, 3.083 and 3.644. Your numbers will differ; expect the same ordering of direct against NTK-aware, and PI without fine-tuning no better than direct.
traps: Applying position interpolation in the wrong direction. YaRN v3 Equation 9 writes \(g(m) = s \cdot m\) with \(s = L'/L\), which would stretch positions; its own Appendix A.1 Equation 16 and the PI paper use \(m L / L' = m / s\). Divide by \(s\).

Taking the Modern LLM Notebook's Section 10 as YaRN. It describes NTK base change plus a per-dimension temperature, while YaRN's temperature is one scalar on all logits and the per-dimension step is the frequency ramp of NTK-by-parts. The notebook's `ExtrapolatableRoPE` implements the `yarn` strategy as NTK-aware only and marks it as simplified.

Calling a method 'extended' from one perplexity number or one passkey test. In the small run in the reproduce step, YaRN's temperature did not help (its loss was slightly above NTK-by-parts at every length), and a 16-pair model is not a Llama. Compare methods at several lengths and seeds, and report whether any fine-tuning happened.

selfTest.q: Show that the RoPE score depends only on \(m - n\).
selfTest.a: Per pair, \(R_{m\theta}^\top R_{n\theta} = R_{(n-m)\theta}\), because rotations are orthogonal and compose by adding angles. So \(\langle R_m q, R_n k\rangle\) is a function of \(q\), \(k\) and \(n - m\) for every pair, hence of the position difference only.

selfTest.q: For head size 128 and base 10000, what base does NTK-aware scaling use for \(s = 8\), and what happens to the first and last pairs' frequencies?
selfTest.a: \(b' = 10000 \cdot 8^{128/126} \approx 82{,}684.6\). The first pair has \(\theta_0 = 1\) either way and is unchanged. The last pair's frequency is multiplied by exactly \(1/8\), as in position interpolation.

selfTest.q: With PI at \(s = 4\), what does the model see for two tokens that are 60 positions apart, and what is the cost?
selfTest.a: They look 15 positions apart, because positions are divided by 4. The model never sees angles beyond the trained range, but all neighbouring tokens are 4 times closer in angle, so local resolution drops. That is the reason a short fine-tune is needed.

selfTest.q: For \(s = 8\), what multiplier does YaRN apply to the attention logits, and how is it implemented without changing the attention code?
selfTest.a: \(1/t = (0.1 \ln 8 + 1)^2 \approx 1.459\) (so \(\sqrt{1/t} \approx 1.208\)). Scale both the queries and the keys by \(\sqrt{1/t}\), for example by scaling the cached rotary cosine and sine tables.

selfTest.q: A model passes a passkey test at 4 times its trained length with a scaled RoPE and no fine-tuning. What else do you need before you say it handles that length?
selfTest.a: Loss or perplexity against length on held-out long documents, tasks that need information spread across the context, the same tests at the trained length (scaling can hurt there), and more than one seed or document set. A single retrieval test shows that one capability exists at that length.

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook: Efficient Attention
study.locator: Sections 2.1 to 2.9 (linear attention, its sharpness cost, SSMs, selective SSM, Mamba-2, Lightning Attention, hybrids)
study.depth: The code in 2.1 and Homework 2 is non-causal, and the 'fast' form in 2.1 reuses the quadratic normalizer. The Jamba row in 2.9 says '24 Mamba : 8 Attention' and 'one attention layer every 8 layers', which disagree.

focus: Write each mixer by its state. Softmax attention keeps the whole KV cache, which grows with length. Sliding-window attention keeps the last \(w\) keys and values. Linear attention keeps \(S_t = S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^\top\), a \(d_k \times d_v\) matrix, and reads \(y_t = S_t^\top q_t\). A Mamba-2 style layer adds a scalar gate, \(S_t = \gamma_t S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^\top\). The delta rule \(S_t = \gamma_t (I - \beta_t k_t k_t^\top) S_{t-1} + \beta_t k_t v_t^\top\) can erase what a key already holds.

The duality is exact for the scalar-gate case. The recurrent form and the masked-matrix form \(Y = (L \circ C B^\top) X\) with \(L_{ts} = \gamma_{s+1} \cdots \gamma_t\) compute the same function, so you can train in the matrix or chunked form and decode with the recurrence. Section 5.1 states the result for a scalar times identity \(A\); it is not a statement about every selective SSM.

A fixed state stores a bounded number of associations. With \(d_k\) orthonormal keys the read returns each value exactly; a repeated key adds to the old value in linear attention (reading it returns the sum), while the delta rule overwrites it. Gates decide what is forgotten. Softmax attention can look up any earlier token, so recall is where hybrids keep a few full-attention layers.

The cost you quote must name the form. The reordering \(Q(K^\top V)\) is valid without a causal mask. With the mask it becomes a scan, or chunks inside which you use the matrix form, as in Listing 1. FLOPs are linear in length for the scan, but the chunked algorithm is what makes it fast on matrix hardware.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, show that \(\sum_{s \le t} (q_t \cdot k_s) v_s\) equals \(q_t^\top S_t\) for \(S_t = \sum_{s \le t} k_s v_s^\top\), and extend it to the gated form with \(L_{ts}\) above. Then run the chunked algorithm of Listing 1 against a plain recurrence in float64 for \(B = 2\), \(T = 16\), 3 heads, head size 5, state size 4, log-gates \(A_t = -u\) with \(u\) uniform in \([0, 1)\), chunk length 4. Outputs and final state should agree to about 1e-15 (1.8e-15 and 8.9e-16 in my run, PyTorch 2.14.1 on CPU), chunk lengths 4 and 8 should agree with each other, the masked-matrix form should agree with the recurrence, and splitting the sequence in two and passing the first final state as `initial_states` to the second call should reproduce the full run. Finally check the interference example: keys \(e_1, e_2, e_1\) with values \(v_1, v_2, v_3\) (the unit vectors of 3 dimensions). Reading \(e_1\) gives \([1, 0, 1]\) in linear attention and \([0, 0, 1]\) under the delta rule with \(\gamma = \beta = 1\).
traps: Using the unmasked reordering for a decoder. For random \(Q, K, V\) with 6 tokens, \((QK^\top \text{ masked}) V\) and \(Q(K^\top V)\) differ in every row but the last. Test the causal identity row by row, and test that changing a future token leaves earlier outputs unchanged.

Reading 'Transformers are SSMs' as 'any SSM equals attention'. The duality needs the scalar-gate structure, and the result says nothing about quality. A model with a fixed state compared with softmax attention at equal parameters can still fail recall tasks. Test with an associative-recall or copy task, not only loss.

Treating a hybrid's gain as an architecture result without controls. Slide 11 of Lecture 4 says there are few controlled ablations; a published hybrid changes layer ratio, depth, width and data together. Hold parameters, tokens and sequence length fixed and vary one thing.

selfTest.q: Per head, what is the decoding state of softmax attention, sliding-window attention with window \(w\), and linear attention, and how does the per-token decoding cost scale in each?
selfTest.a: Softmax attention: keys and values for all \(T\) past tokens, cost \(O(T d)\) per token. Sliding window: the last \(w\) keys and values, \(O(w d)\). Linear attention: one \(d_k \times d_v\) matrix, \(O(d_k d_v)\), independent of \(T\).

selfTest.q: For the gated recurrence \(S_t = \gamma_t S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^\top\), write the matrix \(M\) with \(Y = MX\).
selfTest.a: \(M_{ts} = (q_t \cdot k_s) \prod_{r=s+1}^{t} \gamma_r\) for \(s \le t\) and 0 otherwise. The product of gates is the 1-semiseparable mask \(L\), and \(M = L \circ (C B^\top)\) in the paper's notation.

selfTest.q: Why does the reordering of slide 4 not apply directly to a causal decoder?
selfTest.a: The causal mask zeroes the entries above the diagonal of \(QK^\top\) before multiplying by \(V\). The matrix \(K^\top V\) sums over all positions, including future ones, so \(Q(K^\top V)\) leaks the future. The causal version is a running sum, either a scan or a chunked algorithm.

selfTest.q: A layer with state \(d_k \times d_v\) with \(d_k = 2\) has stored two associations with orthonormal keys. What does a third write with a new key do in linear attention and in the delta rule?
selfTest.a: The new key lies in the span of the two existing ones, so its value adds into the same state entries. Reads of the old keys are perturbed in linear attention. The delta rule first removes what the new key already retrieves, which changes the old reads as well. A fixed state cannot keep more independent associations than its key dimension.

selfTest.q: Name three things a hybrid-versus-attention comparison must hold fixed.
selfTest.a: Parameters (or compute) counted from the actual models, training tokens and data order, and sequence length, plus the optimizer and learning-rate tuning budget for each arm. It also needs a recall-sensitive evaluation next to loss, and more than one seed.

focus: Two router conventions. Switch and DeepSeek's first models take a softmax over all \(E\) experts, then the top-\(k\) probabilities as gate values. Mixtral-style routers take the top-\(k\) logits, then a softmax over just those. They agree for \(k \ge 2\) only up to a renormalization, and they differ in an important way at \(k = 1\): a softmax over one logit is the constant 1, so the router gets no gradient from the language-model loss.

Capacity is a per-expert, per-batch limit: \(C = \lceil \text{cf} \cdot k\,T / E \rceil\) for \(T\) tokens in the group that shares the buffer. Switch's Equation 3 is the \(k = 1\) case; with top-\(k\) there are \(kT\) assignments to spread over \(E\) experts. A token that arrives after an expert is full is not computed for that expert, and passes on through the residual connection. Which tokens lose a slot is a rule you must choose and test, for example token order within the group.

A drop is silent. The loss still goes down, so track the dropped fraction per layer and per batch. Switch reports under 1% with its balancing loss. Because capacity is shared across the batch, a token's output can depend on its neighbours; Lecture 4 slide 47 points out that other requests can drop your token.

Expert parallelism sends tokens to the device that holds their expert and brings the results back, so each MoE layer does two all-to-alls in the forward pass and two in the backward pass. With fixed-size capacity buffers the payload is set by the capacity, not by the actual routing, and only the fraction \((P-1)/P\) leaves the device.
units.reproduce: By hand, route 8 tokens to 4 experts with top-1 assignments \([0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3]\), counts \([5, 1, 1, 1]\). With capacity factor 1.0 the capacity is 2, tokens 2, 3 and 4 are dropped, and the dropped fraction is 0.375. With 1.25 the capacity is \(\lceil 2.5 \rceil = 3\) and tokens 3 and 4 are dropped (0.25). With 2.5 the capacity is 5 and nothing is dropped. Then derive the payload for 8192 tokens per device, width 4096, bfloat16, \(k = 2\), capacity factor 1.25 and 8 expert-parallel devices: \(1.25 \cdot 2 \cdot 8192 \cdot 4096 \cdot 2 \cdot \tfrac{7}{8} = 146{,}800{,}640\) bytes, exactly 140 MiB, per all-to-all per device. Finally implement dispatch (position in expert from a cumulative sum of the assignment mask), expert computation on the gathered tokens, and combine with gate weights, and check it against a per-token loop with the capacity set high enough that nothing drops. In float32 on random inputs the two should agree to about 1e-6.
traps: Using a softmax over the selected logits when \(k = 1\). In a 6-token, 8-wide toy router (PyTorch 2.14.1), the gate values were exactly 1.0 and the summed absolute gradient of the router weights was 0.0, against 46.2 when the softmax was taken over all experts before the top-1. TensorTonic's router returns weight 1 for \(k = 1\) because it renormalizes over the selected experts, which is correct for its statement and has this consequence.

Testing an MoE layer for causality or batch independence with capacity pressure on. A dropped token makes a layer's output depend on which other tokens share the buffer, and a priority by router score can let a later token take an earlier token's slot. Turn drops off (capacity at least \(T\)) for equivalence tests, and test the drop path separately with a fixed priority rule.

Counting capacity from tokens rather than assignments for \(k > 1\), or forgetting that two assignments of one token go to different experts. Check that a token's \(k\) experts are distinct, and that the sum of the dispatched counts equals \(kT\) minus the drops.

selfTest.q: A group has 4096 tokens, 64 experts, \(k = 2\) and a capacity factor of 1.25. What is the expert capacity?
selfTest.a: \(\lceil 1.25 \cdot 2 \cdot 4096 / 64 \rceil = 160\) tokens per expert. The ideal load is 128 assignments per expert, and the factor adds a 25% buffer.

selfTest.q: Eight tokens are assigned to experts \([0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3]\) with capacity 3 and token order as priority. Which tokens are dropped and what is the dropped fraction?
selfTest.a: Tokens 3 and 4, the fourth and fifth arrivals at expert 0, so the fraction is 2/8 = 0.25. The other tokens fit, since experts 1 to 3 hold one token each.

selfTest.q: Why does a top-1 router with a softmax over the selected logit never learn from the language-model loss, and what fixes it?
selfTest.a: The gate value is \(\operatorname{softmax}\) of one number, which is always 1, so the output has no dependence on the router logits except through the discrete choice, which has no gradient. Take the softmax over all experts first and multiply the expert output by the selected probability, as Switch does, or use a balancing loss as the only router signal (which is not enough by itself).

selfTest.q: Give the all-to-all payload per device for 4096 tokens, width 2048, bfloat16, \(k = 1\), capacity factor 1.0 and 4 devices. Does a more balanced router change it with fixed buffers?
selfTest.a: \(1.0 \cdot 1 \cdot 4096 \cdot 2048 \cdot 2 \cdot \tfrac{3}{4} = 12{,}582{,}912\) bytes (12 MiB) per all-to-all. With fixed-size buffers, no: the payload is set by the capacity. Balance changes how many slots hold real tokens and how many are padding.

selfTest.q: Why must a causal-prefix test of an MoE layer run with drops disabled?
selfTest.a: With drops, a token's output depends on the other tokens competing for the same expert buffer. Under a rule that lets a later token take a slot from an earlier one, a future token can change a past token's output, which breaks prefix invariance by design of the dispatch rule, not by a mask bug. With capacity at least the token count nothing is dropped, and the layer is a function of each token alone.

focus: Log from hooks on detached tensors, every few steps, and keep the numbers as Python floats. Per layer: the root mean square of the residual stream, the gradient norm of one weight per sublayer, and the maximum attention logit. Per run: the mean of \(\log Z\) over output logits. A hook that keeps a tensor with its graph leaks memory, and one that calls `.item()` every layer every step adds synchronizations.

OLMo 2 summarizes growth with \(\lambda = \frac{1}{n_{\text{layers}}} \log\left(\|v'\| / \|v\|\right)\), where \(v\) and \(v'\) are the average activation (or gradient) vectors at the first and last layer. A constant per-layer gain \(g\) gives \(\lambda = \log g\), so ideal is 0. It averages over documents and positions, so also compute it at several sequence lengths and note that it hides a profile that rises then falls.

Choose the oracle per property. Prefix invariance is exact in the same shapes (0.0 in my run). Position-offset invariance is exact in real arithmetic but not in floating point, because the rotation angle is the product of the position and the frequency, so its error grows with the offset. Padding invariance needs an attention mask for left padding. Gradient checks need a float64 path with no hard-coded float32 inside.

A test that cannot fail proves nothing. For each property, seed one defect (flipped mask, ignored offset, angles in float32, wrong group mapping, norm over the wrong axis) and check the test goes red, then remove it. The A1 tests compare outputs with stored snapshots of the baseline model. They pin the baseline against regression and do not test causality or offsets directly.
units.reproduce: On a tiny decoder (vocabulary 64, width 32, 2 layers, 4 query heads, 2 KV heads, FFN width 64, RoPE, RMSNorm, random weights), implement the battery and run it. Labeled example, not a target (PyTorch 2.14.1, CPU): changing the last 12 of 24 tokens left the first 12 logits identical (difference 0.0) in float32 and float64; flipping the mask made the same test fail with a difference of 2.02. Shifting all positions by 0, 1000, 4096 and 100000 changed float64 logits by 0, 7.6e-15, 2.4e-14 and 9.5e-13, and float32 logits differed from the float64 reference by 8.2e-7, 4.7e-6, 2.0e-5 and 5.2e-4. Computing the angles in float32 inside a float64 model reproduced that 5.2e-4 error at offset 100000 and the offset test caught it. Random content in right padding changed nothing (0.0); left padding with correct position ids but no attention mask changed the real tokens' logits by 1.87. Float64 finite-difference checks on entries of a key projection (step 1e-6, central differences) gave relative errors of 2.3e-9, 1.3e-8 and 1.6e-9. Your values will differ; the pattern to reproduce is exact zero, error that grows with the offset in float32, and every seeded defect going red.
traps: One tolerance for every test. In float32 the position-offset error is about 8e-7 at offset 0 and 5e-4 at offset 100000, so a fixed 1e-5 either fails a correct model at long offsets or is too loose to catch a defect at short ones. Set the tolerance from the offset and the dtype, and compare against a float64 reference.

A float64 gradient check through a stack that upcasts internally. In my toy, a norm and a softmax that cast to float32 gave relative errors of 0.07 to 1.0 on the same entries that gave 1e-9 after the casts were made dtype-aware. The check measured float32 noise, not the gradient. Promote to at least float32 (`torch.promote_types`), not to exactly float32.

Calling padding handled because right padding passes. A causal mask alone makes right padding harmless. Left padding changes which keys are visible, so it needs an attention mask as well as shifted position ids.

selfTest.q: Per-layer activation norm grows by a factor of 1.05 each layer in a 48-layer model. What is the growth exponent and what is the ratio of last-layer to first-layer norm?
selfTest.a: \(\lambda = \log 1.05 \approx 0.049\) and the ratio is \(1.05^{48} \approx 10.4\). A small positive exponent compounds into an order of magnitude over depth.

selfTest.q: Why can't a RoPE position-offset test demand exact equality in float32 at offset 100000, and what is the spacing of float32 numbers near that angle?
selfTest.a: The angle is position times frequency, about \(10^5\) for the fastest pair, and float32 numbers in \([65536, 131072)\) are spaced \(2^{-7} \approx 0.0078\) apart. The angle is rounded, so cosine and sine change by up to a few thousandths. The offset-0 and offset-100000 logits cannot be equal, only close.

selfTest.q: A batch is left-padded and the position ids are shifted to start at 0 on the first real token. Real-token logits still differ from the unpadded run. Why?
selfTest.a: The pad tokens are still valid keys for every later query, because the causal mask only hides the future. Without an attention mask that hides the pad keys, they change the attention weights. Right padding is safe because the pads come after every real token.

selfTest.q: Name two properties that an MoE layer with dropped tokens will violate, and the settings under which they hold.
selfTest.a: Batch independence and causal prefix invariance can fail, because a token's output depends on the other tokens that share expert capacity. They hold when capacity is at least the token count so nothing is dropped, or when the dropping rule is fixed and causal.

selfTest.q: You see a finite-difference relative error of 0.4 on a single weight entry. List two causes to rule out before you suspect the backward pass.
selfTest.a: Float32 operations inside the forward path (noise larger than the step times the gradient), and a step size or an entry whose gradient is near zero. Also check dropout and other randomness, and weight aliasing from expanded or shared tensors.

focus: A special-case table is the unit of work. GQA with \(n_{kv} = n_h\) is MHA, and with \(n_{kv} = 1\) is MQA. Copying each group's key and value weights to all its query heads turns GQA into an MHA that computes exactly the same function. An MoE whose experts are all copies of one dense feed-forward network equals it when the gate weights sum to 1 and nothing is dropped. MLA with a latent of width \(2 n_h d_h\) (no compression, no RoPE) equals MHA. RoPE scaling at \(s = 1\) equals the baseline. A gated scan with gate 1 equals causal linear attention.

Load the same weights, not the same seed. Write one function per pair that maps the baseline state dictionary to the variant state dictionary, then compare logits and gradients. The first mismatch is usually a layout error: `repeat` against `repeat_interleave` gives the same shapes and a different function.

Test the lossy direction by what it must preserve. Mean pooling heads into groups changes the function, so do not assert equality with the original. Assert instead that the converted model equals an MHA whose heads inside each group are all set to the group mean.

The tolerance belongs to the weakest link. A router that computes its softmax in float32 makes an otherwise float64 MoE-versus-dense test agree only to about 1e-8. Gates that you renormalize must sum to 1 to the precision of that softmax.
units.reproduce: Write the state-dictionary maps and run these checks in float64 on a tiny model (width 32, 4 heads, FFN width 48, 6 experts, PyTorch 2.14.1 on CPU). Labeled example: GQA with 2 KV heads against the replicated 4-head MHA, difference 0.0; the same copy with `repeat` in place of `repeat_interleave`, difference 2.32; MHA against mean-pooled GQA, 1.44 (not equal, as expected); NTK-aware base and position interpolation at \(s = 1\), 0.0, with the YaRN temperature factor exactly 1; MHA against MLA with latent width \(2 n_h d_h = 64\) and the up-projections set to the two halves of the identity, 0.0; the gated scan with gate 1 against causal linear attention, 1.8e-15. For the MoE with 6 identical experts and renormalized top-2 and top-3 gates, the difference to the dense network was 1.4e-8 and 1.9e-8, limited by the float32 router; with top-1 and the raw probability as gate, the output was the dense output times the selected probability (ratio 0.18 to 0.22).
traps: Comparing two models built from the same seed instead of the same weights. Different module layouts consume random numbers in a different order, and the test fails or, worse, passes by luck of a symmetric initialization. Always build the variant by mapping the baseline's state dictionary.

Demanding exactness where the variant is lossy or the gate does not sum to 1. Top-1 routing with a raw probability gate gives \(p\) times the dense output by design, and mean-pooled heads are not the original heads. Write the expected relation, not the identity you wish held.

Passing a shape check and calling the transfer done. Equal shapes hide wrong head order, wrong axis in the pooled mean and a missing scale. Compare logits and at least one gradient on inputs with nonzero positions and a causal mask.

selfTest.q: Which conversion between MHA and GQA is exact, and how do you build it?
selfTest.a: GQA to MHA. Copy each group's key and value projection rows to every query head in the group, in contiguous order, and keep the query and output projections. The MHA then computes the same attention as the GQA model. The other direction needs mean pooling plus training.

selfTest.q: An MoE layer has 8 identical experts and top-2 routing with softmax over all experts followed by renormalization over the two selected. When does it equal the dense layer with the same weights?
selfTest.a: When no token is dropped, because then each token's output is the sum of two weights that add to 1 times the same dense output. With capacity pressure a dropped assignment removes part of the sum, and with unnormalized gates the output is the sum of the selected probabilities times the dense output.

selfTest.q: What latent width makes MLA without RoPE reproduce an MHA layer, and what are the up-projections?
selfTest.a: \(2 n_h d_h\), the full width of the keys and values together. The down-projection stacks the key and value projections of the MHA, and the key and value up-projections select the first and second half. Any narrower latent compresses and cannot reproduce arbitrary MHA weights.

selfTest.q: Why is it wrong to test MHA against a mean-pooled GQA for equality, and what can you assert?
selfTest.a: Averaging heads changes the keys and values each query sees, so the function changes. Assert that the converted GQA equals an MHA whose heads in each group are replaced by the group mean, and that shapes, parameter counts and KV bytes are what the formulas say.

selfTest.q: Your float64 MoE-versus-dense test agrees to 1e-8 and not 1e-14. Where do you look first?
selfTest.a: For operations inside the path that run in float32, such as a router computed in float32 for stability. The gate weights then sum to 1 only to about 1e-8. Either make the router dtype-aware for the test or set the tolerance to the router's precision.
